_comment: WHAT A PERSON EATS, AND WHAT CHANGES IT.
Every number a household's grocery basket is built from lives here and
nowhere else. Consumption.java reads it and answers the questions; nothing
else holds a copy. See that file's header for the two laws these numbers
are shaped to obey.
UNITS. A kilogram, and money in the game's thousands - so 0.0070 is $7.00 a
kilo, which is what imported meat costs. Prices are the WORLD's, delivered
and at the gate, the same two ends every other good in this game is priced
at. Nothing here is made locally yet; that is the next batch.
kcalPerUnit is per kilogram and is what subsistence is measured in, so the
cheapest calorie in the file is the floor a starving household collapses
to. quality is 0 to 1 and is nutrition, not price. elasticity is the income
elasticity of demand - NEGATIVE for an inferior good, which is what a
staple is: a household eats LESS rice as it gets richer, and that is the
whole of Bennett's law. convenience is 0 to 1, where 1 is food that needs
no cooking. referenceKg is what one person eats in a month at the reference
income, which is what every other quantity is scaled from.
THIRTEEN IS A STARTING POINT AND THE FILE IS BUILT FOR A THOUSAND. Goods
are addressed BY KEY everywhere, never by position, so adding or removing a
row cannot shift anything else - the same rule the save format learned the
hard way in September.
_targetComment: WHAT A BALANCED DIET LOOKS LIKE, as a share of calories by category.
Diet quality is not the average healthiness of what is in the basket - by
that measure a famine diet of eighty per cent grain scores WELL, because
there is nothing wrong with rice. It is the DISTANCE FROM BALANCE, which
is how every real diet-quality index is built, and it is the only shape
that penalises both ends: too much starch because the household is poor,
and too many treats because it is rich.
Roughly a healthy mixed diet - about half the calories from staples, a
quarter from protein, and the rest split between produce, prepared food
and treats. The shares sum to one and the harness asserts it.

goods.label: Grains
goods.note: Rice, pasta, flour. The cheapest calorie in the file at 4,500 kcal a dollar, so it is what a household with nothing eats and what it stops eating first when it can afford to.

goods.label: Bread
goods.note: A staple that needs no cooking, which is why it is only mildly inferior where grains are strongly so.

goods.label: Dairy and eggs
goods.note: The cheapest protein, so it is the first thing a household buys on the way up and the last protein it gives up on the way down.

goods.label: Vegetables
goods.note: Almost no calories for the money, which is exactly why a household short of food buys grain instead - and why a city that eats no vegetables is not a city that is starving.

goods.label: Meat
goods.note: Bennett's law in one row: the share of a city's calories that comes from meat is the single best guess at how rich it is.

goods.label: Cooking fats
goods.note: The densest calorie in the file by a factor of two. A household buying calories rather than food buys grain and oil, which is what every real famine diet looks like.

goods.label: Ready meals
goods.note: The convenience axis at its far end: bought for time rather than for money, which is why a working household with children buys it and an out-of-work household with the same children does not.

goods.label: Bakery goods
goods.note: Cake, not bread. Kept apart from BREAD deliberately - one is a staple a household eats more of when it is poor and the other is a treat it eats more of when it is rich, and a single 'baked goods' row cannot say both.

goods.label: Drinks
goods.note: Non-alcoholic, for now. Alcohol and tobacco are their own categories when there is an excise dial to put on them.
